nodes.label: Hindu-Arabic numerals
nodes.place: India; via Baghdad (al-Khwarizmi, c. 825) to Italy (Fibonacci, 1202)
nodes.desc: Place-value digits with a zero, worked out in India by about the 6th century, taken up in Abbasid Baghdad and carried to Italy by Fibonacci's Liber Abaci (1202). Written arithmetic on paper replaced the counting board for merchants, and made long ledgers, interest and exchange sums quick to check.

nodes.label: Magnetic compass
nodes.place: Song China (navigation by about 1100); Europe and the Indian Ocean by about 1190
nodes.desc: A magnetised needle that shows north in cloud and out of sight of land. Used by Song pilots by about 1100, known in the Mediterranean by the 1190s; it let ships keep sailing in winter overcast and, with charts, made ocean crossings and set seasons of shipping more regular.

nodes.label: Cannon founding
nodes.place: Yuan China (c. 1288); Europe from the 1320s; cast-iron guns in the Weald from 1543
nodes.desc: Casting gun barrels from bronze by bell-founders, then from cheap blast-furnace iron. Needed gunpowder, a foundry and a state buyer; it made war a matter of money and furnaces, and naval and siege guns drove iron demand until Wilkinson bored cannon from the solid (1774), the method that bored Watt's cylinders (part 07).

nodes.label: Handguns and muskets
nodes.place: Europe and the Ottoman empire; later the US armouries
nodes.desc: Hand-held guns (matchlock from about 1450, flintlock from about 1610) that made infantry with little training effective. Made by gunsmiths in towns, then in state armouries, where the American system of interchangeable parts was worked out (part 07); guns were also a main trade good for furs and captives.

nodes.label: Caravels and carracks
nodes.place: Portugal and Castile
nodes.desc: Ocean-going ships combining northern hulls and square sails with the Mediterranean lateen sail, navigated by compass and latitude sailing. They carried the Portuguese down Africa, to India (1498) and across the Atlantic, and with them sugar, captives, silver, crops and disease (part 11).

nodes.label: Movable-type press
nodes.place: Mainz (Gutenberg); earlier movable type in Song China (Bi Sheng, 1040s) and Korea (1377)
nodes.desc: Cast metal type set in a screw press and printed on rag paper. By 1500 Europe had printed perhaps 20 million copies; cheap print carried price lists, arithmetic and bookkeeping manuals (Pacioli, 1494), technical books and later newspapers.

nodes.label: European porcelain
nodes.place: Meissen (Saxony); Sevres; Wedgwood's Etruria, Stoke
nodes.desc: European kilns imitating the Chinese porcelain imported by the East India companies: Delft tin-glaze, true porcelain at Meissen (1710), Wedgwood's creamware at Etruria (1769). The pottery works became one of the first centralised manufactories, with fine division of labour and clocking-in (part 07).

nodes.label: Water-powered silk throwing
nodes.place: Lucca and Bologna; copied at Derby (Lombe, 1721)
nodes.desc: Water-driven machines that twisted reeled silk into thread on hundreds of spindles at once, guarded as a trade secret in Lucca and Bologna. Lombe's copy at Derby (1721) was a powered precursor of the cotton factory (part 07).

nodes.label: Fustian (cotton-linen)
nodes.place: northern Italy; south Germany (Barchent) from the 1370s; Lancashire from about 1600
nodes.desc: Cloth with a linen warp and a cotton weft, made from cotton imported from the Levant. It moved from Italy to the Augsburg and Ulm putting-out trades and then to Lancashire, where the fustian makers were the industry that mechanised cotton spinning grew out of.

nodes.label: European calico printing
nodes.place: London; Mulhouse; Lancashire (Peel's)
nodes.desc: Printing fast colours on cotton with mordants and wood blocks, learned from Indian chintz, then with copper rollers (1783). Protected by the Calico Acts' ban on Indian prints, it grew into the Lancashire finishing trade that bought bleach and dyes (part 07).

nodes.label: Turkey red dyeing
nodes.place: Ottoman and Indian method; Rouen (1747); Vale of Leven, Scotland (1785)
nodes.desc: A long, oil-and-alum mordant madder process giving a fast bright red on cotton, brought from the Levant and India by Greek dyers to France and then to Glasgow. The Vale of Leven Turkey-red works were a main finishing trade (part 07) until synthetic alizarin (1868).

nodes.label: Tobacco plantations
nodes.place: Virginia and Maryland (Chesapeake)
nodes.desc: An American crop (part 11) grown for export in Virginia from 1612, first by indentured servants and then by enslaved Africans. It exhausted soils and pushed settlement west, and its customs revenue and the Glasgow and London tobacco merchants tied the colony to European finance.

nodes.label: Coffee trade
nodes.place: Yemen (Mocha); then Java, Saint-Domingue and Brazil
nodes.desc: An Ethiopian plant grown in Yemen and shipped through the Red Sea (part 11 lists it among Old World crops sent to the Americas). Europe's coffee houses (London 1652) drank it first from Mocha, then from Dutch Java and the slave plantations of the Caribbean and Brazil.

nodes.label: Canton tea trade
nodes.place: Canton (Guangzhou) to London and Amsterdam
nodes.desc: Chinese tea bought at Canton for silver by the East India companies, the largest of their China imports by the mid-18th century. Silver bought silk, porcelain and tea (part 11); the drain of silver to pay for tea was later reversed by Bengal opium.

nodes.label: Cassava in Africa
nodes.place: Kongo and West Africa, from Brazil
nodes.desc: An American root (part 11: a famine crop and staple in central Africa) brought from Brazil by the Portuguese. It grows on poor soil and keeps in the ground, so it fed people through drought and war, and as flour it victualled slave ships.

nodes.label: American epidemic collapse
nodes.place: the Americas
nodes.desc: Smallpox, measles and influenza from the Old World killed about 56 million people in the Americas by 1600, roughly 90 per cent (Koch and others 2019, contested in detail; part 11). The collapse emptied land for plantations and cattle and left a labour shortage filled by forced labour and the Atlantic slave trade.

nodes.label: Japanese silver (Iwami)
nodes.place: Iwami Ginzan and other Japanese mines
nodes.desc: Silver mined in Japan from the 1520s and refined by cupellation brought from Korea (1533). With American silver it supplied China, whose money and taxes ran on silver after paper failed (part 11); Portuguese and Chinese ships carried it to the mainland.

nodes.label: Murano glass
nodes.place: Murano, Venice
nodes.desc: Venice's glass industry, moved to Murano in 1291, using Levantine plant-ash soda and Syrian methods; clear cristallo (c. 1450) and mirrors. Its guild kept the secrets by law, and its skills and workers were later lured to France and England.

nodes.label: Jacquard loom
nodes.place: Lyon
nodes.desc: A loom attachment that lifts warp threads by a chain of punched cards, replacing the drawloom's draw-boy for patterned silk. Its cards were the model for Babbage's engine and Hollerith's census tabulator.

nodes.label: Carolina rice plantations
nodes.place: South Carolina and Georgia lowcountry
nodes.desc: Tidal wet-rice fields on slave plantations, worked with the rice skills of enslaved West Africans (Carney, contested in degree). With indigo it made the Carolina lowcountry one of the richest slave economies.
